pages.title: Device and cable
pages.for: The device protects the cable. Choose the device from Ib, then the cable from the device, where the cable runs hottest: Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz. The cable must also take the current that finally operates the device: I2 ≤ 1.45 Iz. Both come from Regulation 433.1.1.
pages.rule:
Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz, and I2 ≤ 1.45 Iz
It ≥ In ÷ (Ca × Cg × Ci × Cf), only the factors that act together
Iz = tabulated figure × the same factors, except Cf
BS 3036 fuse: Cf = 0.725 (1.45 ÷ 2)

Work It for each part of the run. Design to the highest, on the reference method that cuts Iz most.
Cg counts the circuit itself. A cable at no more than 30% of its grouped rating may be left out (Table 4C1 note 9).
BS EN 60898 breakers and BS 88 fuses meet I2 ≤ 1.45 Iz once Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz holds (Regulation 433.1.201).
A motor's thermal relay: In is its setting. Check its own curve.

traps.text: Multiplying factors that never act together, or designing to the easier section or reference method. On the heater circuit, 24.18 A is wrong and 21.28 A is right.
Leaving the circuit being installed out of Cg.
A rewireable fuse without Cf: its I2 can pass the cable's 1.45 Iz.
traps.cite: Slides p.25; Professional Electrician (NICEIC), in research

traps.text: Sizing a star-delta motor's six cables on the line current: they carry a winding's current.
traps.cite: Pack p.4 (delta running conditions); Schneider Electric and Siemens, in research

traps.text: Reading 90 °C ratings when the starter's or motor's terminals are designed for less. Rate the cables at the terminals' temperature: at 70 °C, 1.5 mm² carries only 15.5 A.
traps.cite: Table 4E1A note 1; Table 4D1A column 5 (your copy p.448, 458)

pages.name: Do you still have it?
pages.task: A heater circuit has In 16 A. The whole run is in a warm room, Ca 0.94. The cable is clipped direct, then runs in trunking with another circuit, Cg 0.8. Then it leaves the trunking and passes through a cavity wall with 50 mm of thermal insulation, Ci 0.88. What tabulated current It must the cable have?
pages.alt: 16 ÷ (0.94 × 0.8) = 21.28 A, the worse of the two places. You may see it printed as 21.2 A, cut short. 24.18 A is the usual slip: it multiplies factors that never act together. 19.34 A is the easier place.
pages.html:
16 ÷ (0.94 × 0.8) = 21.28 A, the worse of the two places.

You may see it printed as 21.2 A, cut short. 24.18 A is the usual slip: it multiplies factors that never act together. 19.34 A is the easier place.

pages.name: What it is for
pages.text: Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz. The device's rating is at least the design current. Where it runs, the cable carries at least the device's rating. I2 is the current that finally operates the device. It is no more than 1.45 Iz.
pages.alt: REGULATION 433.1.1 Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz In ≥ Ib: the device's rating or current setting is at least the design current. Iz ≥ In: the cable's current-carrying capacity, where it is installed, is at least the device's. The table's figure, It, is for a single circuit at the table's ambient. Iz is what the cable carries continuously where it actually runs. I2 ≤ 1.45 Iz One more condition. I2, the current that finally operates the device, is no more than 1.45 Iz. If it is skipped or wrong: a cable that makes heat faster than it can shed runs hot.
pages.html:
Regulation 433.1.1

Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz

In ≥ Ib: the device's rating or current setting is at least the design current.

Iz ≥ In: the cable's current-carrying capacity, where it is installed, is at least the device's.

The table's figure, It, is for a single circuit at the table's ambient. Iz is what the cable carries continuously where it actually runs.

I2 ≤ 1.45 Iz

One more condition. I2, the current that finally operates the device, is no more than 1.45 Iz.

If it is skipped or wrong: a cable that makes heat faster than it can shed runs hot. Over time that damages insulation, joints, terminations and their surroundings.

pages.name: The why: the run in sections
pages.text: The trunking sets the cable at 21.28 A. You get 24.18 A only if all three factors act in one place.
pages.alt: The heater circuit, In 16 A, drawn as its route in three sections. Clipped Ca 0.94 It 17.02 A Trunking Ca 0.94 Cg 0.8 It 21.28 A Insulated wall Ca 0.94 Ci 0.88 It 19.34 A Sets the cable In trunking with another circuit: the warm room and the grouping act together. 0.94 × 0.8 = 0.752 16 ÷ 0.752 = 21.28 A The trunking needs the most, 21.28 A, so it sets the cable. There the warm room starts the cable warmer, and the other circuit stops it shedding its heat. The wall needs 19.34 A and the clipped part 17.02 A. The reference method sets the table column too.
pages.html:
The heater circuit, In 16 A, drawn as its route in three sections.

In trunking with another circuit: the warm room and the grouping act together.

0.94 × 0.8 = 0.752

16 ÷ 0.752 = 21.28 A

The trunking needs the most, 21.28 A, so it sets the cable. There the warm room starts the cable warmer, and the other circuit stops it shedding its heat. The wall needs 19.34 A and the clipped part 17.02 A.With insulation inside the trunking too, all three act in one place. So the trunking needs 24.18 A. This is the one place where multiplying all three is right.

The reference method sets the table column too. This run has two methods: B in the trunking and C clipped direct. Design to B, the one that cuts Iz most. The wall has no column of its own here.

Cg always counts the circuit being installed.

You may ignore a cable expected to carry not more than 30% of its grouped rating. Leave it out when finding the factor for the rest of the group (Table 4C1 note 9).

pages.text: A 10 A breaker's 14.50 A is within the 13 A cable's 18.85 A. A 10 A rewireable fuse reaches 20.00 A and needs a cable with Iz of 13.79 A.

Device: 10 A rewireable fuse 0 A 25 A In 10 A I2 20.00 A Iz 13.79 A 1.45 Iz 20.00 A Cable: the size this fuse needs Passes with Iz 13.79 A: the 13 A cable is too small behind this fuse Divide the fuse's 10 A by Cf, and you need a cable with Iz 13.79 A. Breakers to BS EN 60898 and fuses to BS 88 meet I2 ≤ 1.45 Iz whenever Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz holds (Regulation 433.1.201). The breaker here does. A rewireable fuse needs Cf. A motor's thermal relay is checked on its maker's curve.

pages.name: Section A (c)
pages.task: The showroom's motor has a design current of 23.08 A, from part (a). (c) Determine the smallest standard rating of the circuit-breaker at DBP2 for the motor circuit.
pages.alt: Your showroom: the motor SCENARIO A newly built car retailer; cars are driven over the showroom's concrete floor. Supply: three phase four wire 400 V, TN-C-S, Ze declared as 0.1 Ω, prospective fault current 4.6 kA; ambient 20 °C. Five boards: MDB, DBL1, DBL2, DBP1 and DBP2. In the consultation bay, a 400 V three-phase 11 kW motor, power factor 0.8 lagging, efficiency 86%, controlled by a star-delta starter and not subject to frequent starting and stopping. The cables from the starter to the motor are 90 °C thermosetting singles in conduit.
pages.html:
Your showroom: the motorScenario

A newly built car retailer; cars are driven over the showroom's concrete floor. Supply: three phase four wire 400 V, TN-C-S, Ze declared as 0.1 Ω, prospective fault current 4.6 kA; ambient 20 °C. Five boards: MDB, DBL1, DBL2, DBP1 and DBP2. In the consultation bay, a 400 V three-phase 11 kW motor, power factor 0.8 lagging, efficiency 86%, controlled by a star-delta starter and not subject to frequent starting and stopping. The cables from the starter to the motor are 90 °C thermosetting singles in conduit.

Your assignment ED4-01A: pack p.3, and question 4 on p.4.

Carried forward
(a)Motor's design current, Ib23.08 A
(b)Each winding, in delta13.33 A

Given: the standard ratings near Ib are 16, 20, 25 and 32 A.

23.08 A ≤ 25 A, the smallest standard rating not below it (20 A is below)

The type. A motor takes much more current starting than running. A star-delta start draws roughly 2 to 2.7 times full-load current. Direct-on-line draws 6 to 8 times. These are rough guide figures, not a standard. Take 2.7 here, a practice value: 2.7 × 23.08 = 62.32 A. Use the motor maker's figure on a real job.

Type B, 3 to 5 In: 75 to 125 A

Type C, 5 to 10 In: 125 to 250 A

Type D, 10 to 20 In: 250 to 500 A

Which type of breaker suits the practice start of 62.32 A?

Type C.

Type C suits small motors. We take it here because it clears the start with more room than B.

Then the overload. We assume the starter's thermal relay sits in the delta circuit. There it is set to 0.58 × the motor's full-load current, from the nameplate. 0.58 is 1 ÷ √3, rounded. It is never set higher than the phase current: 23.08 ÷ √3 = 13.33 A. That setting is the In of the starter-to-motor cables.

Given: the room is at 20°C. Six 90 °C thermosetting singles run from the starter to the motor, sized on the delta running conditions. They share one conduit on the consultation bay's wall. We assume it is clear of insulation, so Ci and Cf are 1.

First: how many circuits do the six singles count as for Cg?

Two circuits.

In delta running, all six carry winding current. For three-phase circuits, n singles count as n/3 circuits of three loaded conductors (Table 4C1 note 5).

6 ÷ 3 = 2 circuits; Table 4C1 item 1, two circuits bunched and enclosed: Cg 0.80.

Take Ca as 1.00 here, a practice value. It takes no credit for the cool 20 °C room. Table 4B1 covers ambients other than 30 °C. Its first row, 25 °C, gives 1.02 for 90 °C thermosetting. On a real job, check Table 4B1 for how to treat 20 °C.

13.33 ÷ (1.00 × 0.80) = 16.66 A

Non-armoured 90 °C thermosetting singles are in Table 4E1A. Conduit on a wall is Reference Method B. Two three-phase circuits read the 3 or 4 cables column.

Table 4E1A, column 5

Read column 5 in your copy of the table.

1 mm²: 15 A < 16.66 A, no; 1.5 mm²: 20 A ≥ 16.66 A

Column 5: 1 mm² carries 15 A, under 16.66 A. 1.5 mm² carries 20 A, the smallest that passes.

Check the terminals. These are 90 °C ratings. They hold only if the starter's and motor's terminals are designed for 90 °C. If they are designed for less, rate the cables at the terminals' temperature (Table 4E1A note 1). At 70 °C, Table 4D1A column 5 gives 1.5 mm² only 15.5 A, under 16.66 A.

Iz = 20 × 1.00 × 0.80 = 16.00 A; Ib 13.33 ≤ In 13.33 ≤ Iz 16.00

Iz 16.00 A is below the 25 A breaker at DBP2. So for these cables, that breaker gives protection against fault current only. Lesson 7 checks that.

Regulation 433.1.201 does not list thermal relays, as step 4 showed. So read the relay's curve from its maker. It must operate by 1.45 × 16.00 = 23.20 A.

A conduit fixed to a masonry wall may carry more. We take no credit for that here.

pages.name: Section B
pages.task: State a hazard of an overload current in a circuit, and explain how the design keeps a small overload from harming the cable.
pages.why: A model answer: An overload makes the circuit conductors run hotter than the temperature they were chosen for. Over time that damages the insulation, joints and terminations and what surrounds them. It can lead to fire. The design guards the cable first with Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz. Then it adds I2 ≤ 1.45 Iz. The current that finally makes the device operate must not exceed 1.45 times the cable's current-carrying capacity. So a small overload that lasts until the device opens does not deteriorate the cable. A rewireable fuse to BS 3036 can need up to about twice its rating to operate. So its rating is kept to 0.725 Iz, which is Cf.
